segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I wish you would put up with a little foolishness from me. But in fact you are putting up with me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I am jealous for you with God's own jealousy, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I am afraid that somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your minds may be corrupted and turned from single-minded and pure devotion to Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus, whom we did not proclaim, or you receive a different spirit, which you did not receive, or different good news, which you did not accept, you put up with it well enough.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I reckon that I fall short of those super-apostles in nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Even if I am untrained in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I proclaimed God's good news to you free of charge?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I robbed other assemblies, taking pay from them so as to serve you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when I was with you and ran short, I was a burden to no one, for the brothers who came from Macedonia made up my shortfall. In everything I kept myself from weighing on you, and I will keep doing so.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As the truth of Christ is in me, this boast of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I am doing I will go on doing, so as to cut off the opportunity from those who want an opportunity to be found on the same footing as we are in what they boast about.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And no wonder, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So it is no great thing if his servants also disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will be according to their works.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I say again, let no one think me a fool. But if you do, then accept me even as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I am saying I am not saying according to the Lord, but as in foolishness, in this undertaking of boasting.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you gladly put up with fools, wise as you are!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you put up with it if someone enslaves you, if someone devours you, if someone takes advantage of you, if someone exalts himself, if someone strikes you in the face.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To my shame I say it: we were too weak for that! But wherever anyone else is daring (I am speaking in foolishness), I am daring too.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they Abraham's offspring? So am I.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Are they servants of Christ? I am talking like a madman: I am more so. In labors far more, in prisons far more, in beatings beyond measure, in danger of death often.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Five times I received from Jews the forty lashes less one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I have spent adrift on the open sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On journeys often, in dangers from rivers, dangers from bandits, dangers from my own people, dangers from Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in labor and toil, in sleepless nights often, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and without enough clothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me, my anxiety for all the assemblies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If boasting is necessary, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In Damascus the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.

notes.phrase: you are putting up with me
notes.note: The Greek verb form can be either a statement ('you are putting up with me') or a command ('do put up with me'). Many translations choose the command. The statement is taken here because the preceding wish is phrased as something not yet happening, which the 'but in fact' then corrects; either reading is defensible.

Some manuscripts lack the words 'and the purity', reading only 'from the single-mindedness that is toward Christ'. The longer reading has strong early support and is printed in the SBLGNT, but the words could have dropped out or been added by accident because the two Greek nouns end alike. The word rendered 'single-minded' is often translated 'simplicity' or 'sincerity'; it denotes undivided loyalty.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for a welcome announcement, and the related verb in verse 7 ('proclaimed ... good news') shares its root. 'Gospel' is the customary English and is not wrong, but it now suggests a book or a genre. Several modern translations also use 'good news'.

Paul's phrase is literally 'the exceedingly-beyond apostles', and the same expression recurs at 12:11. Most scholars take it as sarcasm aimed at the rival missionaries in Corinth, whom he calls false apostles in verse 13. A minority think it refers, without sarcasm, to the leading apostles in Jerusalem, to whom the rivals appealed.

The Greek word meant a gathering of people: a city's citizen assembly, and in the Greek Old Testament the assembled people of Israel. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is always visible.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. The traditional 'righteousness' is kept here, but the reader should hear in it both doing what is right and being in the right.

Most translations render this 'confidence of boasting'. The sense 'confidence' is thinly attested for this word in the period, and recent lexical work favours 'project, undertaking' or 'situation' here and at 9:4. The matter remains disputed, and the traditional rendering is still widely defended.

Deuteronomy 25:3 limits a flogging to forty strokes. Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine so that a miscount could not break the law. This was a synagogue punishment, which means Paul kept submitting to synagogue discipline as a Jew. None of the five occasions is recorded in Acts.

Beating with rods was a punishment ordered by Roman magistrates, as distinct from the synagogue lashes of verse 24. Acts 16:22-23 records one instance, at Philippi. Roman citizens were legally exempt from it, though the exemption was not always honoured.

The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'. In the plural, in Jewish usage, it means the non-Jewish peoples. This translation uses 'Gentiles' for the latter sense and 'nations' for the former; they are the same Greek word. Here it stands opposite 'my own people', that is, fellow Jews.

notes.traditional: Beside those things that are without
notes.note: The phrase can mean 'apart from the things left unmentioned' or 'apart from external things', that is, the outward hardships just listed. The first is the more common view today and is followed here. The word rendered 'pressure' also has a manuscript variant, and its sense ranges from 'pressure' to 'attention' or 'what comes upon me'; the general meaning is not affected.

notes.traditional: the governor under Aretas the king
notes.note: Aretas IV ruled the Nabataean kingdom, south and east of Judea, until about AD 40, which makes this one of the few fixed points for dating Paul's life. The official's title is 'ethnarch'. Whether he governed Damascus for Aretas or was the head of the Nabataean community there is disputed. Acts 9:23-25 tells the same escape.

'According to the flesh' recurs across Paul; translators differ between 'flesh', 'human standards', 'sinful nature' and 'worldly', and readers are misled when it varies.
Recurs in the Gospels and Paul with renderings ranging over 'offend', 'cause to sin', 'cause to stumble' and 'fall away'; it needs one decision by sense.
The plural is used both for specific male co-workers and for mixed communities; a rule is needed for when 'brothers and sisters' applies.
